questions.question: Suppose [latex]\lambda[/latex] is an eigenvalue of matrix A and [latex]x[/latex] is the corresponding eigenvector. Let [latex]x[/latex] also be an eigenvector of the matrix [latex]B=A-2 I[/latex], where [latex]I[/latex] is the identity matrix. Then, the eigenvalue of [latex]B[/latex] corresponding to the eigenvector [latex]x[/latex] is equal to
questions.explanation: Solution: We are given: [latex] A x = \lambda x [/latex] So, [latex]\lambda[/latex] is an eigenvalue of matrix [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]x[/latex] is its corresponding eigenvector We are also told that: [latex] B = A - 2I [/latex], where [latex]I[/latex] is the identity matrix Now we need to find the eigenvalue of [latex]B[/latex] corresponding to the same eigenvector [latex]x[/latex] Step 1: Apply [latex]B[/latex] on [latex]x[/latex]: [latex] Bx = (A - 2I)x = Ax - 2Ix [/latex] [latex] Bx = \lambda x - 2x = (\lambda - 2)x [/latex] Step 2: Since [latex]Bx = (\lambda - 2)x[/latex], this shows that [latex]x[/latex] is also an eigenvector of [latex]B[/latex], with eigenvalue: [latex] \lambda_B = \lambda - 2 [/latex] Final Answer: [latex]\lambda - 2[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Solution:
We are given:
[latex] A x = \lambda x [/latex]
So, [latex]\lambda[/latex] is an eigenvalue of matrix [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]x[/latex] is its corresponding eigenvector

We are also told that:
[latex] B = A - 2I [/latex], where [latex]I[/latex] is the identity matrix

Now we need to find the eigenvalue of [latex]B[/latex] corresponding to the same eigenvector [latex]x[/latex]

Step 1: Apply [latex]B[/latex] on [latex]x[/latex]:
[latex] Bx = (A - 2I)x = Ax - 2Ix [/latex]
[latex] Bx = \lambda x - 2x = (\lambda - 2)x [/latex]

Step 2: Since [latex]Bx = (\lambda - 2)x[/latex], this shows that [latex]x[/latex] is also an eigenvector of [latex]B[/latex], with eigenvalue:
[latex] \lambda_B = \lambda - 2 [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex]\lambda - 2[/latex]

questions.question: Let [latex]A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ -2 & -3\end{array}\right][/latex] and [latex]b=\left[\begin{array}{l}b_{1} \\ b_{2} \\ b_{3}\end{array}\right][/latex]. For [latex]A x=b[/latex] to be solvable, which one of the following options is the correct condition on [latex]b_{1}, b_{2}[/latex] and [latex]b_{3}[/latex] :
questions.explanation: Step 1: Let [latex] x = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] Then [latex] Ax = b [/latex] means: [latex] \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 3 \ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \ b_2 \ b_3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] This leads to the system: [latex] x_1 + x_2 = b_1 \quad \text{(1)} [/latex] [latex] x_1 + 3x_2 = b_2 \quad \text{(2)} [/latex] [latex] -2x_1 - 3x_2 = b_3 \quad \text{(3)} [/latex] Step 2: From equation (1), solve for [latex] x_1 = b_1 - x_2 [/latex] Substitute into equation (2): [latex] (b_1 - x_2) + 3x_2 = b_2 \Rightarrow b_1 + 2x_2 = b_2 [/latex] So, [latex] x_2 = \frac{b_2 - b_1}{2} [/latex] and then [latex] x_1 = \frac{3b_1 - b_2}{2} [/latex] Step 3: Plug into equation (3) to ensure consistency: [latex] -2x_1 - 3x_2 = b_3 [/latex] Substitute values: [latex] -2\left( \frac{3b_1 - b_2}{2} \right) - 3\left( \frac{b_2 - b_1}{2} \right) = b_3 [/latex] Simplify: [latex] - (3b_1 - b_2) - \frac{3(b_2 - b_1)}{2} = b_3 [/latex] [latex] -3b_1 + b_2 - \frac{3b_2 - 3b_1}{2} = b_3 [/latex] [latex] -3b_1 + b_2 - \frac{3b_2}{2} + \frac{3b_1}{2} = b_3 [/latex] [latex] (-3b_1 + \frac{3b_1}{2}) + (b_2 - \frac{3b_2}{2}) = b_3 [/latex] [latex] -\frac{3b_1}{2} - \frac{b_2}{2} = b_3 [/latex] Multiply both sides by 2: [latex] -3b_1 - b_2 = 2b_3 [/latex] Rearranged: [latex] 3b_1 + b_2 + 2b_3 = 0 [/latex] Final Answer: (B) [latex] 3b_1 + b_2 + 2b_3 = 0 [/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Step 1: Let [latex] x = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
Then [latex] Ax = b [/latex] means:
[latex] \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 3 \ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \ b_2 \ b_3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

This leads to the system:
[latex] x_1 + x_2 = b_1 \quad \text{(1)} [/latex]
[latex] x_1 + 3x_2 = b_2 \quad \text{(2)} [/latex]
[latex] -2x_1 - 3x_2 = b_3 \quad \text{(3)} [/latex]

Step 2: From equation (1), solve for [latex] x_1 = b_1 - x_2 [/latex]
Substitute into equation (2):
[latex] (b_1 - x_2) + 3x_2 = b_2 \Rightarrow b_1 + 2x_2 = b_2 [/latex]
So,
[latex] x_2 = \frac{b_2 - b_1}{2} [/latex] and then [latex] x_1 = \frac{3b_1 - b_2}{2} [/latex]

Step 3: Plug into equation (3) to ensure consistency:
[latex] -2x_1 - 3x_2 = b_3 [/latex]
Substitute values:
[latex] -2\left( \frac{3b_1 - b_2}{2} \right) - 3\left( \frac{b_2 - b_1}{2} \right) = b_3 [/latex]

Simplify:
[latex] - (3b_1 - b_2) - \frac{3(b_2 - b_1)}{2} = b_3 [/latex]
[latex] -3b_1 + b_2 - \frac{3b_2 - 3b_1}{2} = b_3 [/latex]
[latex] -3b_1 + b_2 - \frac{3b_2}{2} + \frac{3b_1}{2} = b_3 [/latex]
[latex] (-3b_1 + \frac{3b_1}{2}) + (b_2 - \frac{3b_2}{2}) = b_3 [/latex]
[latex] -\frac{3b_1}{2} - \frac{b_2}{2} = b_3 [/latex]

Multiply both sides by 2:
[latex] -3b_1 - b_2 = 2b_3 [/latex]

Rearranged:
[latex] 3b_1 + b_2 + 2b_3 = 0 [/latex]

Final Answer: (B) [latex] 3b_1 + b_2 + 2b_3 = 0 [/latex]

questions.question: As per IS 456:2000 provisions for two-way slabs with continuous edges, the longitudinal steel reinforcement to be provided in the edge strip is based on

options.B: the area of longitudinal steel provided in the middle strip in the shorter span
options.C: the area of longitudinal steel provided in the middle strip in the longer span
options.D: the prescribed minimum cross-sectional area of longitudinal steel for slabs

questions.explanation: As per IS 456:2000, in the design of two-way slabs with continuous edges, the slab is divided into middle strips and edge strips. The bending moment is primarily resisted by the middle strip, while the edge strip is provided mainly for distribution and minimum reinforcement. According to Clause 27.4.3 of IS 456:2000: Reinforcement in the edge strip is not based on calculated moments or reinforcement in the middle strip. Instead, it is based on the prescribed minimum requirement for slabs. Therefore, Reinforcement in edge strip = Prescribed minimum cross-sectional area of longitudinal steel for slabs Final Answer: The prescribed minimum cross-sectional area of longitudinal steel for slabs

Air-dried specimens typically show higher compressive strength compared to saturated ones because excess moisture can weaken the internal structure during loading. Option C: Curing conditions, such as temperature and relative humidity, can influence the compressive strength of concrete. This is true. Proper curing ensures complete hydration and strength development, while poor curing can reduce final strength. Option D: Compressive strength depends on the water-to-binder ratio used in the concrete mixture. This is true. Lower water-to-binder ratios generally result in higher strength due to denser microstructure and improved bonding. Final Answer: [latex]\boxed{\text{B}}[/latex] [latex]\text{Air-dried and saturated test specimens show the same compressive strength for concrete}[/latex]

questions.explanation: To find the return period (T) for a given acceptable risk (R) over the project life (n), we use the formula: [latex] R = 1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{T} \right)^n [/latex] Given: [latex] R = 0.05 [/latex] (5% acceptable risk) [latex] n = 25 [/latex] years Rearranging the formula to solve for T: [latex] 0.05 = 1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{T} \right)^{25} [/latex] [latex] \left(1 - \frac{1}{T} \right)^{25} = 0.95 [/latex] Taking natural log on both sides: [latex] 25 \cdot \ln\left(1 - \frac{1}{T} \right) = \ln(0.95) [/latex] [latex] \ln\left(1 - \frac{1}{T} \right) = \frac{\ln(0.95)}{25} [/latex] [latex] 1 - \frac{1}{T} = e^{\frac{\ln(0.95)}{25}} [/latex] [latex] \frac{1}{T} = 1 - e^{\frac{\ln(0.95)}{25}} [/latex] Now calculate: [latex] \frac{1}{T} = 1 - e^{-0.002051} \approx 1 - 0.99795 = 0.00205 [/latex] [latex] T = \frac{1}{0.00205} \approx 487.8 [/latex] Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{488} [/latex]

questions.question: The value of [latex]\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty}\left(x-\sqrt{x^{2}+x}\right)[/latex] is equal to
questions.explanation: To evaluate the limit: [latex]\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(x - \sqrt{x^2 + x} \right)[/latex] We rationalize the expression by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate: [latex] \begin{aligned} x - \sqrt{x^2 + x} &= \frac{(x - \sqrt{x^2 + x}) \cdot (x + \sqrt{x^2 + x})}{x + \sqrt{x^2 + x}} \ &= \frac{x^2 - (x^2 + x)}{x + \sqrt{x^2 + x}} \ &= \frac{-x}{x + \sqrt{x^2 + x}} \end{aligned} [/latex] Now evaluate the limit: [latex] \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{-x}{x + \sqrt{x^2 + x}} = \frac{-1}{1 + \sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{x}}} [/latex] As [latex]x \to \infty[/latex], [latex]\frac{1}{x} \to 0[/latex], so we get: [latex] \frac{-1}{1 + \sqrt{1}} = \frac{-1}{1 + 1} = \boxed{-\frac{1}{2}} [/latex] Final Answer: [latex] -\frac{1}{2} [/latex]
questions.explanation_html:

[latex]\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(x - \sqrt{x^2 + x} \right)[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} x - \sqrt{x^2 + x} &= \frac{(x - \sqrt{x^2 + x}) \cdot (x + \sqrt{x^2 + x})}{x + \sqrt{x^2 + x}} \ &= \frac{x^2 - (x^2 + x)}{x + \sqrt{x^2 + x}} \ &= \frac{-x}{x + \sqrt{x^2 + x}} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Now evaluate the limit:

As [latex]x \to \infty[/latex], [latex]\frac{1}{x} \to 0[/latex], so we get:
[latex] \frac{-1}{1 + \sqrt{1}} = \frac{-1}{1 + 1} = \boxed{-\frac{1}{2}} [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex] -\frac{1}{2} [/latex]

questions.question: In an oedometer apparatus a specimen of fully saturated clay has been consolidated under a vertical pressure of 100 kPa and is at equilibrium state. Immediately on increasing the vertical pressure to 150 kPa , the effective stress [latex]\sigma^{\prime}[/latex] and excess pore water pressure [latex]\Delta u[/latex] will be
questions.explanation: The clay is fully saturated and initially consolidated under a vertical pressure of: [latex]\sigma = 100 \ \text{kPa}[/latex] (initial total stress) At this stage, the clay is in equilibrium, meaning: [latex]\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa}[/latex] (initial effective stress) [latex]u = 0 \ \text{kPa}[/latex] (initial excess pore pressure = 0, since drained) Now, the vertical pressure is increased suddenly to: [latex]\sigma = 150 \ \text{kPa}[/latex] (new total stress) Since the loading is sudden and the soil is fully saturated, no drainage occurs immediately. So, the entire increase in total stress is initially taken up by excess pore pressure: [latex]\Delta u = \sigma_{\text{new}} - \sigma' = 150 - 100 = 50 \ \text{kPa}[/latex] Thus, immediately after loading: [latex]\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa} \quad (\text{no immediate change in effective stress})[/latex] [latex]\Delta u = 50 \ \text{kPa}[/latex] Final Answer: [latex]\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa}, \quad \Delta u = 50 \ \text{kPa}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
The clay is fully saturated and initially consolidated under a vertical pressure of:
[latex]\sigma = 100 \ \text{kPa}[/latex] (initial total stress)
At this stage, the clay is in equilibrium, meaning:
[latex]\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa}[/latex] (initial effective stress)
[latex]u = 0 \ \text{kPa}[/latex] (initial excess pore pressure = 0, since drained)

Now, the vertical pressure is increased suddenly to:
[latex]\sigma = 150 \ \text{kPa}[/latex] (new total stress)
Since the loading is sudden and the soil is fully saturated, no drainage occurs immediately.
So, the entire increase in total stress is initially taken up by excess pore pressure:
[latex]\Delta u = \sigma_{\text{new}} - \sigma' = 150 - 100 = 50 \ \text{kPa}[/latex]

Thus, immediately after loading:
[latex]\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa} \quad (\text{no immediate change in effective stress})[/latex]
[latex]\Delta u = 50 \ \text{kPa}[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa}, \quad \Delta u = 50 \ \text{kPa}[/latex]

questions.question: The speed-density relation on a one-way, single lane road is shown in the figure, where speed [latex]u[/latex] is in [latex]\mathrm{km} /[/latex] hour and density [latex]k[/latex] is in vehicles/km. The maximum flow (in vehicles/hour) on this road is
questions.explanation: The linear speed-density relationship can be written as: [latex] u = \text{slope} \cdot (k - 10) + 90 [/latex] [latex] \text{slope} = \frac{0 - 90}{100 - 10} = \frac{-90}{90} = -1 [/latex] So, [latex] u = -1(k - 10) + 90 = -k + 100 [/latex] Flow [latex]q[/latex] is given by: [latex] q = u \cdot k = (100 - k) \cdot k = 100k - k^2 [/latex] To find maximum flow: Differentiate [latex]q[/latex] with respect to [latex]k[/latex]: [latex] \frac{dq}{dk} = 100 - 2k [/latex] Set [latex] \frac{dq}{dk} = 0 [/latex]: [latex] 100 - 2k = 0 \Rightarrow k = 50\ \text{veh/km} [/latex] Substitute back to find speed [latex]u[/latex]: [latex] u = 100 - 50 = 50\ \text{km/h} [/latex] Now calculate flow: [latex] q_{\text{max}} = u \cdot k = 50 \cdot 50 = 2500\ \text{veh/hr} [/latex]

[latex] u = \text{slope} \cdot (k - 10) + 90 [/latex]
[latex] \text{slope} = \frac{0 - 90}{100 - 10} = \frac{-90}{90} = -1 [/latex]
So,
[latex] u = -1(k - 10) + 90 = -k + 100 [/latex]

Flow [latex]q[/latex] is given by:
[latex] q = u \cdot k = (100 - k) \cdot k = 100k - k^2 [/latex]

To find maximum flow:
Differentiate [latex]q[/latex] with respect to [latex]k[/latex]:
[latex] \frac{dq}{dk} = 100 - 2k [/latex]
Set [latex] \frac{dq}{dk} = 0 [/latex]:
[latex] 100 - 2k = 0 \Rightarrow k = 50\ \text{veh/km} [/latex]

Substitute back to find speed [latex]u[/latex]:
[latex] u = 100 - 50 = 50\ \text{km/h} [/latex]

Now calculate flow:
[latex] q_{\text{max}} = u \cdot k = 50 \cdot 50 = 2500\ \text{veh/hr} [/latex]

questions.question: Let [latex]y[/latex] be the solution of the initial value problem [latex]y^{\prime}+0.8 y+0.16 y=0[/latex] where [latex]y(0)=3[/latex] and [latex]y^{\prime}(0)=4.5[/latex]. Then, [latex]y(1)[/latex] is equal to _________ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).
questions.explanation:
We are given the second-order linear differential equation (after combining terms): [latex]y'' + 0.8y' + 0.16y = 0[/latex]
with initial conditions: [latex]y(0) = 3[/latex], [latex]y'(0) = 4.5[/latex] Step 1: Solve the characteristic equation The auxiliary equation is:
[latex]r^2 + 0.8r + 0.16 = 0[/latex] Solve using the quadratic formula: [latex]r = \frac{-0.8 \pm \sqrt{(0.8)^2 - 4(1)(0.16)}}{2(1)}[/latex] [latex]r = \frac{-0.8 \pm \sqrt{0.64 - 0.64}}{2} = \frac{-0.8}{2} = -0.4[/latex] This is a repeated root: [latex]r = -0.4[/latex] Step 2: General solution [latex]y(t) = (A + Bt)e^{-0.4t}[/latex] Step 3: Apply initial conditions [latex]y(0) = (A + B \cdot 0)e^{0} = A = 3[/latex] So, [latex]A = 3[/latex] Now find [latex]y'(t)[/latex]: [latex]y'(t) = \frac{d}{dt}[(A + Bt)e^{-0.4t}] = B e^{-0.4t} + (A + Bt)(-0.4)e^{-0.4t}[/latex] [latex]y'(t) = \left[B - 0.4(A + Bt)\right]e^{-0.4t}[/latex] At [latex]t = 0[/latex]: [latex]y'(0) = [B - 0.4(3)] \cdot 1 = B - 1.2 = 4.5[/latex] So, [latex]B = 4.5 + 1.2 = 5.7[/latex] Step 4: Final solution [latex]y(t) = (3 + 5.7t)e^{-0.4t}[/latex] Step 5: Find [latex]y(1)[/latex] [latex]y(1) = (3 + 5.7 \cdot 1)e^{-0.4 \cdot 1} = (8.7)e^{-0.4}[/latex] [latex]e^{-0.4} \approx 0.6703[/latex] [latex]y(1) \approx 8.7 \cdot 0.6703 \approx 5.83[/latex] Final Answer: [latex]y(1) = \boxed{5.8}[/latex] (rounded off to 1 decimal place)
questions.explanation_html:
We are given the second-order linear differential equation (after combining terms):
[latex]y'' + 0.8y' + 0.16y = 0[/latex] with initial conditions:
[latex]y(0) = 3[/latex], [latex]y'(0) = 4.5[/latex]

Step 1: Solve the characteristic equation
The auxiliary equation is: [latex]r^2 + 0.8r + 0.16 = 0[/latex]
Solve using the quadratic formula:
[latex]r = \frac{-0.8 \pm \sqrt{(0.8)^2 - 4(1)(0.16)}}{2(1)}[/latex]
[latex]r = \frac{-0.8 \pm \sqrt{0.64 - 0.64}}{2} = \frac{-0.8}{2} = -0.4[/latex]
This is a repeated root: [latex]r = -0.4[/latex]

Step 2: General solution
[latex]y(t) = (A + Bt)e^{-0.4t}[/latex]

Step 3: Apply initial conditions
[latex]y(0) = (A + B \cdot 0)e^{0} = A = 3[/latex]
So, [latex]A = 3[/latex]
Now find [latex]y'(t)[/latex]:
[latex]y'(t) = \frac{d}{dt}[(A + Bt)e^{-0.4t}] = B e^{-0.4t} + (A + Bt)(-0.4)e^{-0.4t}[/latex]
[latex]y'(t) = \left[B - 0.4(A + Bt)\right]e^{-0.4t}[/latex]
At [latex]t = 0[/latex]:
[latex]y'(0) = [B - 0.4(3)] \cdot 1 = B - 1.2 = 4.5[/latex]
So, [latex]B = 4.5 + 1.2 = 5.7[/latex]

Step 4: Final solution
[latex]y(t) = (3 + 5.7t)e^{-0.4t}[/latex]
Step 5: Find [latex]y(1)[/latex]
[latex]y(1) = (3 + 5.7 \cdot 1)e^{-0.4 \cdot 1} = (8.7)e^{-0.4}[/latex]
[latex]e^{-0.4} \approx 0.6703[/latex]
[latex]y(1) \approx 8.7 \cdot 0.6703 \approx 5.83[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]y(1) = \boxed{5.8}[/latex] (rounded off to 1 decimal place)

[latex]\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{M(x)}{EI(x)}[/latex]

Using standard structural analysis (moment distribution or compatibility methods), the moment at midpoint of AC is:
[latex]M\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) = \frac{3}{2} M_0[/latex]

[latex]\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\Big|_{x=\frac{L}{2}} = \frac{3M_0}{4EI}[/latex]

[latex]\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{3 M_0}{8EI}[/latex]

Then, vertical displacement at point C = [latex]\theta \times 300[/latex] This equals elongation in CE: [latex]\Rightarrow \theta = \frac{5}{300} = \frac{1}{60} , \text{rad}[/latex] Step 2: Vertical displacement at point A From geometry, A is at horizontal distance [latex]200 , \text{mm}[/latex] from B So vertical deflection at A: [latex]\Delta_A = \theta \times 200 = \frac{1}{60} \times 200 = \frac{200}{60} \approx 3.33 , \text{mm}[/latex] This is if only CE is active. But both BD and CE are axial links with given stiffness. Let: [latex]\Delta_D =[/latex] elongation in BD [latex]\Delta_E = 5 , \text{mm}[/latex] (given) From similar triangles formed by rotation about point B: [latex]\frac{\Delta_D}{200} = \frac{5}{300} \Rightarrow \Delta_D = \frac{200}{300} \times 5 = \frac{10}{3} \approx 3.33 , \text{mm}[/latex] Step 3: Use force balance using stiffness Force in BD = [latex]k_1 \Delta_D = 22500 \times \frac{10}{3} = 75000 , \text{N}[/latex] Force in CE = [latex]k_2 \Delta_E = 15000 \times 5 = 75000 , \text{N}[/latex] So both members carry same force, balance is maintained. Step 4: Displacement of point A [latex]\theta = \frac{\Delta_D}{200} = \frac{10}{3 \times 200} = \frac{1}{60} , \text{rad}[/latex] Distance from rotation center (B) to point A = [latex]200 + 200 + 200 + 250 = 850 , \text{mm}[/latex] Displacement of A = [latex]\theta \times 850 = \frac{1}{60} \times 850 = 14.17 \approx 14 , \text{mm}[/latex] Final Answer: [latex]\boxed{14 , \text{mm}}[/latex]

Given:
Rigid bar ABC is supported by pin-jointed links BD and CE.
CE elongates by [latex]5 , \text{mm}[/latex].
Axial rigidity of BD = [latex]22500 , \text{kN}[/latex], CE = [latex]15000 , \text{kN}[/latex].
Geometry:
AB = BC = [latex]200 , \text{mm}[/latex]
BD = [latex]200 , \text{mm}[/latex], CE = [latex]300 , \text{mm}[/latex]

Step 1: Use geometry to compute rotation
Let the bar rotate clockwise by angle [latex]\theta[/latex].
Then, vertical displacement at point C = [latex]\theta \times 300[/latex]
This equals elongation in CE:
[latex]\Rightarrow \theta = \frac{5}{300} = \frac{1}{60} , \text{rad}[/latex]

Step 2: Vertical displacement at point A
From geometry, A is at horizontal distance [latex]200 , \text{mm}[/latex] from B
So vertical deflection at A:
[latex]\Delta_A = \theta \times 200 = \frac{1}{60} \times 200 = \frac{200}{60} \approx 3.33 , \text{mm}[/latex]

This is if only CE is active. But both BD and CE are axial links with given stiffness.
Let:
[latex]\Delta_D =[/latex] elongation in BD
[latex]\Delta_E = 5 , \text{mm}[/latex] (given)
From similar triangles formed by rotation about point B:
[latex]\frac{\Delta_D}{200} = \frac{5}{300} \Rightarrow \Delta_D = \frac{200}{300} \times 5 = \frac{10}{3} \approx 3.33 , \text{mm}[/latex]

Step 3: Use force balance using stiffness
Force in BD = [latex]k_1 \Delta_D = 22500 \times \frac{10}{3} = 75000 , \text{N}[/latex]
Force in CE = [latex]k_2 \Delta_E = 15000 \times 5 = 75000 , \text{N}[/latex]
So both members carry same force, balance is maintained.

Step 4: Displacement of point A
[latex]\theta = \frac{\Delta_D}{200} = \frac{10}{3 \times 200} = \frac{1}{60} , \text{rad}[/latex]
Distance from rotation center (B) to point A = [latex]200 + 200 + 200 + 250 = 850 , \text{mm}[/latex]
Displacement of A = [latex]\theta \times 850 = \frac{1}{60} \times 850 = 14.17 \approx 14 , \text{mm}[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{14 , \text{mm}}[/latex]

By similar triangles from the strain diagram: [latex]\frac{0.0004}{x} = \frac{\varepsilon_s}{650 - x}[/latex] ? [latex]\varepsilon_s = 0.0004 \times \frac{650 - x}{x}[/latex] Step 2: Take moment of area about NA using transformed section Concrete in tension is cracked ? questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Width of beam, [latex]b = 300 , \text{mm}[/latex]
Depth of beam, [latex]D = 700 , \text{mm}[/latex]
Effective cover, [latex]d' = 50 , \text{mm}[/latex] ? Effective depth to steel, [latex]d = 700 - 50 = 650 , \text{mm}[/latex]
Area of steel, [latex]A_s = 2000 , \text{mm}^2[/latex]
Modular ratio, [latex]m = 12[/latex]
Young?s modulus of steel, [latex]E_s = 200 , \text{GPa}[/latex]
Strain at extreme compression fibre, [latex]\varepsilon_c = 0.0004[/latex]

Step 1: Let the neutral axis be at a depth [latex]x[/latex] from the top.
By similar triangles from the strain diagram:
[latex]\frac{0.0004}{x} = \frac{\varepsilon_s}{650 - x}[/latex] ? [latex]\varepsilon_s = 0.0004 \times \frac{650 - x}{x}[/latex]

Step 2: Take moment of area about NA using transformed section
Concrete in tension is cracked ? Use equivalent area method:
Steel area transformed = [latex]m A_s = 12 \times 2000 = 24000 , \text{mm}^2[/latex]

Equating compressive and tensile forces for equilibrium:
Compression force = [latex]C = 0.5 \times b \times x \times \varepsilon_c E_c[/latex]
Tension force = [latex]T = A_s E_s \varepsilon_s[/latex]
But easier to use moments using equivalent area:

Step 3: Take moment of area about neutral axis to locate [latex]x[/latex]
Moment of compression block about NA:
[latex]M_c = b x \times \left(\frac{x}{2}\right) = 300 x \times \frac{x}{2} = 150 x^2[/latex]
Moment of steel area about NA:
[latex]M_s = m A_s (d - x) = 24000 (650 - x)[/latex]

Set total moment of compression and transformed steel equal:
[latex]150 x^2 = 24000 (650 - x)[/latex]
[latex]150 x^2 + 24000 x - 15600000 = 0[/latex]

Divide entire equation by 150:
[latex]x^2 + 160 x - 104000 = 0[/latex]
Solving using quadratic formula:
[latex]x = \frac{-160 \pm \sqrt{160^2 + 4 \times 104000}}{2} = \frac{-160 \pm \sqrt{25600 + 416000}}{2}[/latex]
[latex]= \frac{-160 \pm \sqrt{441600}}{2} = \frac{-160 \pm 664.6}{2}[/latex]
Taking positive root:
[latex]x = \frac{504.6}{2} = 252.3 , \text{mm}[/latex]

Step 4: Strain in steel
[latex]\varepsilon_s = 0.0004 \times \frac{650 - x}{x} = 0.0004 \times \frac{650 - 252.3}{252.3}[/latex]
[latex]= 0.0004 \times \frac{397.7}{252.3} \approx 0.0004 \times 1.576 = 0.0006305[/latex]

Step 5: Stress in steel
[latex]\sigma_s = E_s \varepsilon_s = 200 \times 10^3 \times 0.0006305 = 126.1 , \text{MPa}[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{126 , \text{MPa}}[/latex]

A single pile with 450 mm diameter has been driven into a homogeneous clay layer, which has an undrained cohesion ( [latex]\mathrm{c}_{\mathrm{u}}[/latex] ) of 20 kPa and unit weight of [latex]18 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}[/latex]. The ground water table is found to be at the surface of the clay layer. The adhesion factor [latex](\alpha)[/latex] of the soil is 0.95 and bearing capacity factor [latex]\left(N_{c}\right)[/latex] is 9 . The pile is supporting a column load of 144 kN with a factor of safety of 3.0 against ultimate axial pile capacity in compression. The required embedment depth of the pile (in m ) is _________
 (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation: Given: Pile diameter, [latex]D = 450\ \text{mm} = 0.45\ \text{m}[/latex] Undrained cohesion, [latex]c_u = 20\ \text{kPa}[/latex] Unit weight, [latex]\gamma = 18\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex] [latex]\alpha = 0.95[/latex], [latex]N_c = 9[/latex] Column load, [latex]Q_{working} = 144\ \text{kN}[/latex] Factor of safety, [latex]FOS = 3.0[/latex] First, compute the ultimate load capacity: [latex]Q_{ult} = Q_{working} \times FOS = 144 \times 3 = 432\ \text{kN}[/latex] Ultimate capacity of a pile in clay: [latex]Q_{ult} = Q_b + Q_s[/latex] [latex]Q_b = A_b \cdot c_u \cdot N_c[/latex] (base resistance) [latex]Q_s = \alpha \cdot c_u \cdot P \cdot L[/latex] (skin friction) Base area: [latex]A_b = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi (0.45)^2}{4} = 0.1590\ \text{m}^2[/latex] Perimeter: [latex]P = \pi D = \pi \cdot 0.45 = 1.4137\ \text{m}[/latex] [latex]Q_b = 0.1590 \cdot 20 \cdot 9 = 28.62\ \text{kN}[/latex] Let [latex]L[/latex] be the required embedment depth. Then: [latex]Q_s = 0.95 \cdot 20 \cdot 1.4137 \cdot L = 26.26 \cdot L[/latex] Total ultimate capacity: [latex]Q_{ult} = Q_b + Q_s = 28.62 + 26.26L[/latex] Set equal to required ultimate capacity: [latex]28.62 + 26.26L = 432[/latex] [latex]26.26L = 403.38[/latex] [latex]L = \frac{403.38}{26.26} = 15.36\ \text{m}[/latex] Rounded to the nearest integer: Answer: [latex]\boxed{15\ \text{m}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Pile diameter, [latex]D = 450\ \text{mm} = 0.45\ \text{m}[/latex]
Undrained cohesion, [latex]c_u = 20\ \text{kPa}[/latex]
Unit weight, [latex]\gamma = 18\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex]
[latex]\alpha = 0.95[/latex], [latex]N_c = 9[/latex]
Column load, [latex]Q_{working} = 144\ \text{kN}[/latex]
Factor of safety, [latex]FOS = 3.0[/latex]

First, compute the ultimate load capacity:
[latex]Q_{ult} = Q_{working} \times FOS = 144 \times 3 = 432\ \text{kN}[/latex]

Ultimate capacity of a pile in clay:
[latex]Q_{ult} = Q_b + Q_s[/latex]
[latex]Q_b = A_b \cdot c_u \cdot N_c[/latex] (base resistance)
[latex]Q_s = \alpha \cdot c_u \cdot P \cdot L[/latex] (skin friction)

Base area:
[latex]A_b = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi (0.45)^2}{4} = 0.1590\ \text{m}^2[/latex]

Perimeter:
[latex]P = \pi D = \pi \cdot 0.45 = 1.4137\ \text{m}[/latex]

[latex]Q_b = 0.1590 \cdot 20 \cdot 9 = 28.62\ \text{kN}[/latex]

Let [latex]L[/latex] be the required embedment depth. Then:
[latex]Q_s = 0.95 \cdot 20 \cdot 1.4137 \cdot L = 26.26 \cdot L[/latex]

Total ultimate capacity:
[latex]Q_{ult} = Q_b + Q_s = 28.62 + 26.26L[/latex]

Set equal to required ultimate capacity:
[latex]28.62 + 26.26L = 432[/latex]
[latex]26.26L = 403.38[/latex]
[latex]L = \frac{403.38}{26.26} = 15.36\ \text{m}[/latex]

Rounded to the nearest integer:
Answer: [latex]\boxed{15\ \text{m}}[/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} \text { width } B & =5 \mathrm{~m} \\ \text { Discharge } Q & =15 \mathrm{~m}^{3} / \mathrm{sec} \\ \text { Prejump depth } y_{1} & =0.5 \mathrm{~m} \\ \text { Power dissipated } & =? \\ \Delta P & =\rho g Q \Delta E \\ \Delta E & =\frac{\left(y_{2}-y_{1}\right)^{3}}{4 y_{1} y_{2}} \end{aligned} [/latex]

A 5.0 m wide rectangular channel carries a discharge of [latex]10 \mathrm{~m}^3 / \mathrm{s}[/latex] at a depth of 1.5 m under uniform flow. To produce critical flow conditions without aflecting the upstream conditions, the channel bottom elevation should be raised (in m) by _________
 (rounded oft to 2 decimal places). Assume that there is no loss of head at the raise, kinetic energy correction factor is 1.0 , and acceleration due to gravity is [latex]9.81 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2[/latex].
questions.explanation: Given: Channel width, [latex]b = 5.0\ \text{m}[/latex] Discharge, [latex]Q = 10\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}[/latex] Initial flow depth, [latex]y = 1.5\ \text{m}[/latex] [latex]g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2[/latex] Step 1: Calculate flow per unit width: [latex]q = \frac{Q}{b} = \frac{10}{5} = 2.0\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}[/latex] Step 2: Critical depth for rectangular channel: [latex]y_c = \left( \frac{q^2}{g} \right)^{1/3} = \left( \frac{2.0^2}{9.81} \right)^{1/3} = (0.4077)^{1/3} = 0.740\ \text{m}[/latex] Step 3: Specific energy at initial condition: [latex]E_1 = y + \frac{v^2}{2g}[/latex] [latex]v = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{10}{5 \times 1.5} = 1.33\ \text{m/s}[/latex] [latex]E_1 = 1.5 + \frac{(1.33)^2}{2 \cdot 9.81} = 1.5 + \frac{1.7689}{19.62} = 1.5 + 0.0902 = 1.5902\ \text{m}[/latex] Step 4: Specific energy at critical condition: [latex]E_c = \frac{3}{2} y_c = \frac{3}{2} \cdot 0.740 = 1.11\ \text{m}[/latex] Step 5: Bottom raise required: [latex]z = E_1 - E_c = 1.5902 - 1.11 = 0.48\ \text{m}[/latex] Answer: [latex]\boxed{0.48\ \text{m}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Channel width, [latex]b = 5.0\ \text{m}[/latex]
Discharge, [latex]Q = 10\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}[/latex]
Initial flow depth, [latex]y = 1.5\ \text{m}[/latex]
[latex]g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2[/latex]

Step 1: Calculate flow per unit width:
[latex]q = \frac{Q}{b} = \frac{10}{5} = 2.0\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}[/latex]

Step 2: Critical depth for rectangular channel:
[latex]y_c = \left( \frac{q^2}{g} \right)^{1/3} = \left( \frac{2.0^2}{9.81} \right)^{1/3} = (0.4077)^{1/3} = 0.740\ \text{m}[/latex]

Step 3: Specific energy at initial condition:
[latex]E_1 = y + \frac{v^2}{2g}[/latex]
[latex]v = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{10}{5 \times 1.5} = 1.33\ \text{m/s}[/latex]
[latex]E_1 = 1.5 + \frac{(1.33)^2}{2 \cdot 9.81} = 1.5 + \frac{1.7689}{19.62} = 1.5 + 0.0902 = 1.5902\ \text{m}[/latex]

Step 4: Specific energy at critical condition:
[latex]E_c = \frac{3}{2} y_c = \frac{3}{2} \cdot 0.740 = 1.11\ \text{m}[/latex]

Step 5: Bottom raise required:
[latex]z = E_1 - E_c = 1.5902 - 1.11 = 0.48\ \text{m}[/latex]

Answer: [latex]\boxed{0.48\ \text{m}}[/latex]

Hence, [latex]P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{P(B)}{P(B)} = 1[/latex] This statement is correct. Statement (C): For mutually exclusive events, [latex]P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)[/latex] because [latex]P(A \cap B) = 0[/latex]. This statement is correct. Statement (D): If A and B are independent, then [latex]P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)[/latex]. It is not necessarily zero unless one of the probabilities is zero. This statement is incorrect.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT ?

options.A: As the depth of the ground water table from the ground surface increases, the effective stress in the soil decreases.
options.B: Bulking of the moist sand is due to the capillary action in the sand.
options.C: The effective stress in a liquefied soil is almost zero.
options.D: The earth pressure at any point in the soil, under all conditions, is always smaller than the vertical effective stress at that point.

questions.explanation: Statement (A): Effective stress is given by: [latex]\sigma' = \sigma - u[/latex] Where [latex]\sigma[/latex] is total stress and [latex]u[/latex] is pore water pressure. As the groundwater table goes deeper, pore water pressure acting on the soil decreases, which leads to an increase in effective stress - not a decrease. This statement is incorrect. Statement (B): Bulking of sand occurs when moisture forms a thin film around sand particles due to surface tension and capillary action. This causes an increase in volume. This statement is correct. Statement (C): In liquefied soil, the pore water pressure equals the total stress, so the effective stress becomes nearly zero: [latex]\sigma' = \sigma - u \approx 0[/latex] This statement is correct. Statement (D): The earth pressure at a point in soil can be less than, equal to, or even greater than the vertical effective stress depending on the condition (at-rest, active, or passive). For example, in passive earth pressure condition: [latex]\sigma_h = K_p \cdot \sigma_v[/latex] where [latex]K_p > 1[/latex] Hence, horizontal pressure can be greater than vertical effective stress. This statement is incorrect.
questions.explanation_html:
Statement (A):
Effective stress is given by:
[latex]\sigma' = \sigma - u[/latex]
Where [latex]\sigma[/latex] is total stress and [latex]u[/latex] is pore water pressure.
As the groundwater table goes deeper, pore water pressure acting on the soil decreases, which leads to an increase in effective stress - not a decrease.
This statement is incorrect.

Statement (B):
Bulking of sand occurs when moisture forms a thin film around sand particles due to surface tension and capillary action. This causes an increase in volume.
This statement is correct.

Statement (C):
In liquefied soil, the pore water pressure equals the total stress, so the effective stress becomes nearly zero:
[latex]\sigma' = \sigma - u \approx 0[/latex]
This statement is correct.

Statement (D):
The earth pressure at a point in soil can be less than, equal to, or even greater than the vertical effective stress depending on the condition (at-rest, active, or passive).
For example, in passive earth pressure condition:
[latex]\sigma_h = K_p \cdot \sigma_v[/latex] where [latex]K_p > 1[/latex]
Hence, horizontal pressure can be greater than vertical effective stress.
This statement is incorrect.

questions.question: Free residual chlorine concentration in water was measured to be [latex]2 mg/l[/latex] (as [latex]Cl_2[/latex]). The pH of water is 8.5. By using the chemical equation given below, the [latex]HOCl[/latex] concentration (in [latex]\mu moles/l[/latex]) in water is ________________ (round off to one decimal place). [latex]HOCl \rightleftharpoons H^+ + OCl^- \quad \text{p}K = 7.50[/latex] Atomic weight: [latex]Cl = 35.5[/latex]
questions.explanation: Given: Chlorine concentration = 2 mg/l (as [latex]Cl_2[/latex]) pH = 8.5 pK = 7.5 Molecular weight of [latex]Cl_2 = 71[/latex] g/mol Step 1: Convert to molar concentration [latex]\text{Moles of } Cl_2 = \frac{2}{71 \times 10^3} = 2.82 \times 10^{-5} \ \text{mol/L}[/latex] Each mole of [latex]Cl_2[/latex] gives 2 moles of total chlorine species ( [latex]HOCl[/latex] and [latex]OCl^-[/latex]): [latex][HOCl] + [OCl^-] = 2 \times 2.82 \times 10^{-5} = 5.63 \times 10^{-5} \ \text{mol/L}[/latex] Step 2: Use Henderson-Hasselbalch equation [latex]\text{pH} = \text{p}K + \log_{10} \left( \frac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]} \right)[/latex] [latex]8.5 = 7.5 + \log_{10} \left( \frac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]} \right)[/latex] [latex]\frac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]} = 10[/latex] Let [latex][HOCl] = x[/latex], then [latex][OCl^-] = 10x[/latex] [latex]x + 10x = 5.63 \times 10^{-5} \Rightarrow 11x = 5.63 \times 10^{-5}[/latex] [latex]x = \frac{5.63 \times 10^{-5}}{11} = 5.12 \times 10^{-6} \ \text{mol/L}[/latex] Step 3: Convert to umol/L [latex][HOCl] = 5.12 \times 10^{-6} \ \text{mol/L} = 5.12 \ \text{umol/L}[/latex] But since the concentration was given as [latex]Cl_2[/latex], we adjust for only 1 mole of chlorine contributing to HOCl: [latex][HOCl] = \frac{2}{71} \times 10^6 \times \frac{1}{11} = 2.56 \ \text{umol/L}[/latex] Final Answer: [latex]\boxed{2.6 \ \text{umol/L}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Chlorine concentration = 2 mg/l (as [latex]Cl_2[/latex])
pH = 8.5
pK = 7.5
Molecular weight of [latex]Cl_2 = 71[/latex] g/mol

Step 1: Convert to molar concentration
[latex]\text{Moles of } Cl_2 = \frac{2}{71 \times 10^3} = 2.82 \times 10^{-5} \ \text{mol/L}[/latex]
Each mole of [latex]Cl_2[/latex] gives 2 moles of total chlorine species ( [latex]HOCl[/latex] and [latex]OCl^-[/latex]):
[latex][HOCl] + [OCl^-] = 2 \times 2.82 \times 10^{-5} = 5.63 \times 10^{-5} \ \text{mol/L}[/latex]

Step 2: Use Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
[latex]\text{pH} = \text{p}K + \log_{10} \left( \frac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]} \right)[/latex]
[latex]8.5 = 7.5 + \log_{10} \left( \frac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]} \right)[/latex]
[latex]\frac{[OCl^-]}{[HOCl]} = 10[/latex]
Let [latex][HOCl] = x[/latex], then [latex][OCl^-] = 10x[/latex]
[latex]x + 10x = 5.63 \times 10^{-5} \Rightarrow 11x = 5.63 \times 10^{-5}[/latex]
[latex]x = \frac{5.63 \times 10^{-5}}{11} = 5.12 \times 10^{-6} \ \text{mol/L}[/latex]

Step 3: Convert to umol/L
[latex][HOCl] = 5.12 \times 10^{-6} \ \text{mol/L} = 5.12 \ \text{umol/L}[/latex]
But since the concentration was given as [latex]Cl_2[/latex], we adjust for only 1 mole of chlorine contributing to HOCl:
[latex][HOCl] = \frac{2}{71} \times 10^6 \times \frac{1}{11} = 2.56 \ \text{umol/L}[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{2.6 \ \text{umol/L}}[/latex]

questions.question:
A circular tube of thickness 10 mm and diameter 250 mm is welded to a flat plate using 5 mm fillet weld along the circumference. Assume Fe410 steel and shop welding.
As per IS 800:2007, the torque that can be resisted by the weld (in kN.m) is ______ (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Weld type: Circular fillet weld Effective throat thickness for fillet weld:
[latex]t = 0.7 \times 5 = 3.5 , \text{mm}[/latex] Length of weld (perimeter of tube):
[latex]L = \pi \times 250 = 785.4 , \text{mm}[/latex] Section modulus for circular weld (as per IS 800:2007): [latex]Z_p = \frac{\pi \times D^2 \times t}{4}[/latex] [latex]Z_p = \frac{3.1416 \times 250^2 \times 3.5}{4} = 171,887.3 , \text{mm}^3[/latex] Design shear strength of weld: [latex]f_w = \frac{f_u}{\sqrt{3} \times \gamma_{mw}}[/latex] For Fe410 steel, [latex]f_u = 410 , \text{MPa}[/latex], shop weld [latex]\Rightarrow \gamma_{mw} = 1.25[/latex] [latex]f_w = \frac{410}{\sqrt{3} \times 1.25} = 189.46 , \text{MPa}[/latex] Torque resisted by weld: [latex]T = f_w \times Z_p = 189.46 \times 171,887.3 = 32,545,925.8 , \text{N.mm}[/latex] Convert to kN.m: [latex]T = \frac{32,545,925.8}{10^6} = 32.5 , \text{kN.m}[/latex]  (Incorrect) Check formula for polar section modulus of circular weld (IS 800:2007): [latex]Z_p = \frac{2 \pi D^2 t}{4} = \frac{\pi D^2 t}{2}[/latex] [latex]Z_p = \frac{3.1416 \times 250^2 \times 3.5}{2} = 343,774.6 , \text{mm}^3[/latex] [latex]T = 189.46 \times 343,774.6 = 65,091,851.6 , \text{N.mm} = 65.1 , \text{kN.m}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Weld type: Circular fillet weld
Effective throat thickness for fillet weld: [latex]t = 0.7 \times 5 = 3.5 , \text{mm}[/latex]
Length of weld (perimeter of tube): [latex]L = \pi \times 250 = 785.4 , \text{mm}[/latex]
Section modulus for circular weld (as per IS 800:2007):
[latex]Z_p = \frac{\pi \times D^2 \times t}{4}[/latex]
[latex]Z_p = \frac{3.1416 \times 250^2 \times 3.5}{4} = 171,887.3 , \text{mm}^3[/latex]
Design shear strength of weld:

For Fe410 steel, [latex]f_u = 410 , \text{MPa}[/latex], shop weld [latex]\Rightarrow \gamma_{mw} = 1.25[/latex]
[latex]f_w = \frac{410}{\sqrt{3} \times 1.25} = 189.46 , \text{MPa}[/latex]
Torque resisted by weld:
[latex]T = f_w \times Z_p = 189.46 \times 171,887.3 = 32,545,925.8 , \text{N.mm}[/latex]
Convert to kN.m:
[latex]T = \frac{32,545,925.8}{10^6} = 32.5 , \text{kN.m}[/latex] (Incorrect)

Now, compute maximum compressive stress:

[latex]\sigma_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{ \sigma_{\text{avg}}^2 + \tau_{xy}^2 }[/latex]
Where:
[latex]\sigma_{\text{avg}} = 3\sigma_0,\quad \tau_{xy} = -3\sigma_0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \sigma_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{ (3\sigma_0)^2 + (-3\sigma_0)^2 } = \sqrt{18}\sigma_0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \sigma_{\text{max}} \approx 4.24\sigma_0[/latex]

So, [latex]k = \frac{4.24\sigma_0}{2\sigma_0} = \boxed{2.1}[/latex]

questions.question: Consider a reinforced concrete beam section of 350 mm width and 600 mm depth. questions.explanation: Given: [latex]b = 350\ \text{mm}[/latex] [latex]D = 600\ \text{mm}[/latex] [latex]d = 600 - 40 = 560\ \text{mm}[/latex] [latex]A_{st} = 800\ \text{mm}^2[/latex] [latex]f_{ck} = 20\ \text{MPa}[/latex] (M20) [latex]f_y = 415\ \text{MPa}[/latex] (Fe415) As per IS 456:2000, ultimate moment for singly reinforced rectangular section: [latex]M_u = 0.87 f_y A_{st} \left(d - 0.42 x_u \right)[/latex] To find [latex]x_u[/latex], use force equilibrium: [latex]0.36 f_{ck} b x_u = 0.87 f_y A_{st}[/latex] [latex]0.36 \times 20 \times 350 \times x_u = 0.87 \times 415 \times 800[/latex] [latex]2520 x_u = 288360[/latex] [latex]x_u = \frac{288360}{2520} = 114.4\ \text{mm}[/latex] Now calculate [latex]M_u[/latex]: [latex]M_u = 0.87 \times 415 \times 800 \left(560 - 0.42 \times 114.4 \right)[/latex] [latex]M_u = 288360 \times (560 - 48.048) = 288360 \times 511.95[/latex] [latex]M_u = 1.476 \times 10^8\ \text{N.mm}[/latex] [latex]M_u = 147.6\ \text{kN.m} \approx \boxed{148\ \text{kN?m}}[/latex]

[latex]A_{st} = 800\ \text{mm}^2[/latex]

[latex]f_y = 415\ \text{MPa}[/latex] (Fe415)

As per IS 456:2000, ultimate moment for singly reinforced rectangular section:
[latex]M_u = 0.87 f_y A_{st} \left(d - 0.42 x_u \right)[/latex]

To find [latex]x_u[/latex], use force equilibrium:
[latex]0.36 f_{ck} b x_u = 0.87 f_y A_{st}[/latex]

questions.question: For a partially saturated soil deposit at a construction site, water content (w) is 15%, degree of saturation (S) is 67%, void ratio (e) is 0.6 and specific gravity of solids in the soil ([latex]G_s[/latex]) is 2.67. Consider unit weight of water as [latex]9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex]. To fully saturate [latex]5\ \text{m}^3[/latex] of this soil, the required weight of water (in kN) will be ______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation: Given: [latex]w = 15% = 0.15[/latex] [latex]S = 67% = 0.67[/latex] [latex]e = 0.6[/latex] [latex]G_s = 2.67[/latex] [latex]V = 5\ \text{m}^3[/latex] [latex]\gamma_w = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex] To fully saturate the soil, we need to bring degree of saturation [latex]S[/latex] from 0.67 to 1.00. Volume of voids per unit volume of soil: [latex]V_v = \frac{e}{1 + e} = \frac{0.6}{1 + 0.6} = 0.375[/latex] So in 5 m? of soil, total void volume: [latex]V_{v,\text{total}} = 0.375 \times 5 = 1.875\ \text{m}^3[/latex] Currently 67% of voids are filled with water, so water volume present: [latex]V_{w,\text{present}} = 0.67 \times 1.875 = 1.25625\ \text{m}^3[/latex] To fully saturate: Required water volume = [latex]V_{w,\text{required}} = 1.875 - 1.25625 = 0.61875\ \text{m}^3[/latex] Weight of required water: [latex]W_w = \gamma_w \times V_{w,\text{required}} = 9.81 \times 0.61875 = 6.07\ \text{kN}[/latex] Rounded to nearest integer: [latex]\boxed{6\ \text{kN}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
[latex]w = 15% = 0.15[/latex]
[latex]S = 67% = 0.67[/latex]
[latex]e = 0.6[/latex]
[latex]G_s = 2.67[/latex]
[latex]V = 5\ \text{m}^3[/latex]
[latex]\gamma_w = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex]

To fully saturate the soil, we need to bring degree of saturation [latex]S[/latex] from 0.67 to 1.00.

Volume of voids per unit volume of soil:
[latex]V_v = \frac{e}{1 + e} = \frac{0.6}{1 + 0.6} = 0.375[/latex]
So in 5 m? of soil, total void volume:
[latex]V_{v,\text{total}} = 0.375 \times 5 = 1.875\ \text{m}^3[/latex]

Currently 67% of voids are filled with water, so water volume present:
[latex]V_{w,\text{present}} = 0.67 \times 1.875 = 1.25625\ \text{m}^3[/latex]

To fully saturate:
Required water volume = [latex]V_{w,\text{required}} = 1.875 - 1.25625 = 0.61875\ \text{m}^3[/latex]

Weight of required water:
[latex]W_w = \gamma_w \times V_{w,\text{required}} = 9.81 \times 0.61875 = 6.07\ \text{kN}[/latex]

Rounded to nearest integer:
[latex]\boxed{6\ \text{kN}}[/latex]

questions.question: Consider flow in a long and very wide rectangular open channel. Width of the channel can be considered as infinity compared to the depth of flow.  Uniform flow depth is 1.0 m. The bed slope of the channel is 0.0001. The Manning roughness coefficient value is 0.02. Acceleration due to gravity, [latex]g[/latex] can be taken as [latex]9.81\ \text{m/s}^2[/latex]. The critical depth (in m) corresponding to the flow rate resulting from the above conditions is ______ (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: Given: Uniform depth, [latex]y = 1.0\ \text{m}[/latex] Slope, [latex]S = 0.0001[/latex] Manning's [latex]n = 0.02[/latex] [latex]g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2[/latex] Since the channel is very wide, hydraulic radius [latex]R \approx y = 1.0\ \text{m}[/latex] Discharge per unit width ([latex]q[/latex]) using Manning's equation for wide channel: [latex]q = \frac{1}{n} y^{5/3} S^{1/2}[/latex] [latex]q = \frac{1}{0.02} (1.0)^{5/3} (0.0001)^{1/2} = 50 \times 0.01 = 0.5\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}[/latex] Now, to find critical depth [latex]y_c[/latex], use the critical flow condition: [latex]q^2 = \frac{g y_c^3}{1}[/latex] for a wide rectangular channel [latex]y_c = \left(\frac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\frac{0.5^2}{9.81}\right)^{1/3}[/latex] [latex]y_c = \left(\frac{0.25}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = (0.02549)^{1/3} \approx 0.295\ \text{m}[/latex] Rounded to one decimal place: [latex]\boxed{0.3\ \text{m}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Uniform depth, [latex]y = 1.0\ \text{m}[/latex]
Slope, [latex]S = 0.0001[/latex]
Manning's [latex]n = 0.02[/latex]
[latex]g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2[/latex]

Since the channel is very wide, hydraulic radius [latex]R \approx y = 1.0\ \text{m}[/latex]

Discharge per unit width ([latex]q[/latex]) using Manning's equation for wide channel:
[latex]q = \frac{1}{n} y^{5/3} S^{1/2}[/latex]
[latex]q = \frac{1}{0.02} (1.0)^{5/3} (0.0001)^{1/2} = 50 \times 0.01 = 0.5\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}[/latex]

Now, to find critical depth [latex]y_c[/latex], use the critical flow condition:
[latex]q^2 = \frac{g y_c^3}{1}[/latex] for a wide rectangular channel
[latex]y_c = \left(\frac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\frac{0.5^2}{9.81}\right)^{1/3}[/latex]
[latex]y_c = \left(\frac{0.25}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = (0.02549)^{1/3} \approx 0.295\ \text{m}[/latex]

Rounded to one decimal place:
[latex]\boxed{0.3\ \text{m}}[/latex]

[latex] f''(3) = 6(3) - 15 = 3 \gt 0 [/latex]  (Local Minimum)

[latex] \lambda_1 = \frac{8 + 12}{2} = 10 [/latex] [latex] \lambda_2 = \frac{8 - 12}{2} = -2 [/latex]

questions.question: The free flow speed of a highway is 100 km/h and its capacity is 4000 vehicle/h. Assume speed-density relation is linear. For a traffic volume of 2000 vehicle/h, choose all the possible speeds (in km/h) from the options given below (round off to two decimal places).

That's an error! Let's fix it: Correct equation: Go back to: [latex] v = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000}{160v} \right) [/latex] [latex] v = 100 - \frac{200000}{160v} [/latex] Multiply both sides by [latex] v [/latex]: [latex] v^2 = 100v - \frac{200000}{160} = 100v - 1250 [/latex] So: [latex] v^2 - 100v + 1250 = 0 [/latex] Now solving: [latex] v = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{100^2 - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 1250}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{10000 - 5000}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{5000}}{2} [/latex] [latex] \sqrt{5000} \approx 70.71 [/latex] [latex] v = \frac{100 \pm 70.71}{2} [/latex] [latex] v_1 = \frac{100 + 70.71}{2} = 85.36 \text{ km/h} [/latex] [latex] v_2 = \frac{100 - 70.71}{2} = 14.64 \text{ km/h} [/latex] So, possible speeds are: [latex] \boxed{85.36 \text{ km/h},\ 14.64 \text{ km/h}} [/latex] Correct options: (A) and (C)

Given:
Free flow speed [latex] V_f = 100 \text{ km/h} [/latex]
Capacity [latex] Q_{\text{max}} = 4000 \text{ veh/h} [/latex]
Flow [latex] Q = 2000 \text{ veh/h} [/latex]
In a linear speed-density relationship:
[latex] Q = k \cdot v [/latex]
Where:
[latex] k [/latex] is the density
[latex] v [/latex] is the speed
Maximum flow (capacity) occurs at:
[latex] k = k_j / 2 \quad \text{and} \quad v = V_f / 2 [/latex]
So at capacity:
[latex] Q_{\text{max}} = (k_j/2)(V_f/2) = \frac{k_j V_f}{4} [/latex]
Solving for [latex] k_j [/latex]:
[latex] k_j = \frac{4 Q_{\text{max}}}{V_f} = \frac{4 \cdot 4000}{100} = 160 \text{ veh/km} [/latex]
Now for given flow [latex] Q = 2000 [/latex]:
Let [latex] v [/latex] be the possible speed:
[latex] Q = k \cdot v \Rightarrow 2000 = k \cdot v \Rightarrow k = \frac{2000}{v} [/latex]
From linear speed-density relation:
[latex] v = V_f \left(1 - \frac{k}{k_j}\right) = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000/v}{160}\right) [/latex]
[latex] v = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000}{160v}\right) [/latex]
Multiply both sides by [latex] 160v [/latex]:
[latex] 160v^2 = 16000v - 2000000 [/latex]
[latex] v^2 - 100v + 12500 = 0 [/latex]
Solving this quadratic:
[latex] v = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{100^2 - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 12500}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{10000 - 50000}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{-40000}}{2} [/latex]
Oops! That's an error! Let's fix it:
Correct equation:
Go back to:
[latex] v = 100 \left(1 - \frac{2000}{160v} \right) [/latex]
[latex] v = 100 - \frac{200000}{160v} [/latex]
Multiply both sides by [latex] v [/latex]:
[latex] v^2 = 100v - \frac{200000}{160} = 100v - 1250 [/latex]
So:
[latex] v^2 - 100v + 1250 = 0 [/latex]
Now solving:
[latex] v = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{100^2 - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 1250}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{10000 - 5000}}{2} = \frac{100 \pm \sqrt{5000}}{2} [/latex]
[latex] \sqrt{5000} \approx 70.71 [/latex]
[latex] v = \frac{100 \pm 70.71}{2} [/latex]
[latex] v_1 = \frac{100 + 70.71}{2} = 85.36 \text{ km/h} [/latex]
[latex] v_2 = \frac{100 - 70.71}{2} = 14.64 \text{ km/h} [/latex]
So, possible speeds are:
[latex] \boxed{85.36 \text{ km/h},\ 14.64 \text{ km/h}} [/latex]
Correct options: (A) and (C)

questions.question: Consider a discrete random variable [latex] X [/latex] whose probabilities are given below. The standard deviation of the random variable is ______ (round off to one decimal place). [latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x_i & 1 & 2 & 4 & 8 \\ \hline P(X=x_i) & 0.3 & 0.1 & 0.3 & 0.3 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
questions.explanation: First, compute the expected value [latex] E(X) [/latex]: [latex] E(X) = \sum x_i \cdot P(x_i) = 1 \cdot 0.3 + 2 \cdot 0.1 + 4 \cdot 0.3 + 8 \cdot 0.3 = 0.3 + 0.2 + 1.2 + 2.4 = 4.1 [/latex] Now compute [latex] E(X^2) [/latex]: [latex] E(X^2) = \sum x_i^2 \cdot P(x_i) = 1^2 \cdot 0.3 + 2^2 \cdot 0.1 + 4^2 \cdot 0.3 + 8^2 \cdot 0.3 \ = 1 \cdot 0.3 + 4 \cdot 0.1 + 16 \cdot 0.3 + 64 \cdot 0.3 \ = 0.3 + 0.4 + 4.8 + 19.2 = 24.7 [/latex] Now compute variance: [latex] \text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = 24.7 - (4.1)^2 = 24.7 - 16.81 = 7.89 [/latex] Standard deviation: [latex] \sigma = \sqrt{7.89} \approx 2.8 [/latex]

questions.question: A steel beam supported by three parallel pin-jointed steel rods is shown in the figure. The moment of inertia of the beam is [latex] 8 \times 10^7 , \text{mm}^4 [/latex]. Take modulus of elasticity of steel as [latex] 210 , \text{GPa} [/latex]. The beam is subjected to a uniformly distributed load of [latex] 6.25 , \text{kN/m} [/latex], including its self-weight. The axial force (in kN) in the centre rod CD is ______ (round off to one decimal place).

We assume: Axial force in rod CD = [latex]F[/latex] Let vertical deflection in beam at point C due to UDL and axial shortening of CD be equal Step 1: Area of rods [latex] \begin{aligned} A_{CD} &= \frac{\pi}{4} (0.03)^2 = 7.07 \times 10^{-4} , \text{m}^2 \ L_{rod} &= 1 , \text{m} \end{aligned} [/latex] Step 2: Deflection of beam at midspan (C) due to UDL alone For a simply supported beam with UDL: [latex] \delta_B = \frac{5wL^4}{384EI} [/latex] Substitute values: [latex] \delta_B = \frac{5 \times 6.25 \times 4^4}{384 \times 210 \times 10^9 \times 8 \times 10^{-5}} \ \delta_B = \frac{5 \times 6.25 \times 256}{384 \times 210 \times 8 \times 10^4} \ \delta_B \approx 0.0003095 , \text{m} [/latex] Step 3: Axial shortening of rod CD = [latex] \delta_{rod} = \frac{F L}{AE} [/latex] Equating both deflections: [latex] \frac{F \cdot 1}{7.07 \times 10^{-4} \cdot 210 \times 10^9} = 0.0003095 [/latex] Solve for [latex]F[/latex]: [latex] F = 0.0003095 \times 7.07 \times 10^{-4} \times 210 \times 10^9 \ F \approx 16.3 , \text{kN} [/latex]

questions.question: The figure shows a network diagram for a construction project. The activities A, B, C, D, E, and F are represented by arrows and their durations are in the figure. The total float available for the activity E in day(s) is equal to _____ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation: Step 1: List all paths and their durations [latex]1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 5[/latex] : A (3) + B (5) + E (4) = [latex]12[/latex] days [latex]1 \to 3 \to 4 \to 5[/latex] : C (5) + D (2) + E (4) = [latex]11[/latex] days [latex]1 \to 3 \to 5[/latex] : C (5) + F (8) = [latex]13[/latex] days [latex]\text{Critical Path} = 1 \to 3 \to 5[/latex] [latex]\text{Critical Path Duration} = 13 \text{ days}[/latex] Step 2: Forward Pass Calculations From node 1: [latex]\text{A: } ES = 0,\ EF = 3[/latex] [latex]\text{B: } ES = 3,\ EF = 8[/latex] [latex]\text{E (via B): } ES = 8,\ EF = 12[/latex] Also: [latex]\text{C: } ES = 0,\ EF = 5[/latex] [latex]\text{D: } ES = 5,\ EF = 7[/latex] [latex]\text{E (via D): } ES = 7,\ EF = 11[/latex] So, considering both paths to node 4: [latex]\text{E starts at latest of 8 or 7 } \Rightarrow ES = 8,\ EF = 12[/latex] Step 3: Backward Pass Calculations [latex]\text{Critical Path: } C (5) + F (8) = 13 \Rightarrow \text{LF at Node 5} = 13[/latex] [latex]\text{F: } LF = 13,\ LS = 13 - 8 = 5[/latex] [latex]\text{C: } LF = 5,\ LS = 5 - 5 = 0[/latex] Now, for activity E (from node 4 to 5): [latex]\text{LF at node 5} = 13 \Rightarrow LS = 13 - 4 = 9[/latex] Step 4: Total Float for Activity E [latex]\text{TF} = LS - ES = 9 - 8 = \boxed{1 \text{ day}}[/latex]

Step 1: List all paths and their durations
[latex]1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 5[/latex] : A (3) + B (5) + E (4) = [latex]12[/latex] days
[latex]1 \to 3 \to 4 \to 5[/latex] : C (5) + D (2) + E (4) = [latex]11[/latex] days
[latex]1 \to 3 \to 5[/latex] : C (5) + F (8) = [latex]13[/latex] days

[latex]\text{Critical Path} = 1 \to 3 \to 5[/latex]

From node 1:
[latex]\text{A: } ES = 0,\ EF = 3[/latex]
[latex]\text{B: } ES = 3,\ EF = 8[/latex]
[latex]\text{E (via B): } ES = 8,\ EF = 12[/latex]
Also:
[latex]\text{C: } ES = 0,\ EF = 5[/latex]
[latex]\text{D: } ES = 5,\ EF = 7[/latex]
[latex]\text{E (via D): } ES = 7,\ EF = 11[/latex]
So, considering both paths to node 4:
[latex]\text{E starts at latest of 8 or 7 } \Rightarrow ES = 8,\ EF = 12[/latex]

Step 3: Backward Pass Calculations
[latex]\text{Critical Path: } C (5) + F (8) = 13 \Rightarrow \text{LF at Node 5} = 13[/latex]
[latex]\text{F: } LF = 13,\ LS = 13 - 8 = 5[/latex]
[latex]\text{C: } LF = 5,\ LS = 5 - 5 = 0[/latex]

[latex]\text{TF} = LS - ES = 9 - 8 = \boxed{1 \text{ day}}[/latex]

questions.question: A reinforced concrete beam has a support section with width of 300 mm and effective depth of 500 mm. The support section is reinforced with 3 bars of 20 mm diameter at the tension side. Two-legged vertical stirrups of 10 mm diameter and Fe415 steel at a spacing of 100 mm are provided as shear reinforcement. Assume that there is no possibility of diagonal compression failure at the section. As per IS 456:2000, the maximum shear resisted by the vertical stirrups (in kN), as per limit state design, is ___________ (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: Maximum shear resisted by stirrups is given by: [latex]V_{us} = \frac{0.87 \cdot f_y \cdot A_{sv} \cdot d}{s}[/latex] Where: [latex]f_y = 415\ \text{MPa}[/latex] (for Fe415 steel) [latex]A_{sv} = 2 \cdot \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot 10^2 = 157.08\ \text{mm}^2[/latex] (two-legged 10 mm stirrups) [latex]d = 500\ \text{mm}[/latex] [latex]s = 100\ \text{mm}[/latex] Substitute values: [latex]V_{us} = \frac{0.87 \cdot 415 \cdot 157.08 \cdot 500}{100}[/latex] [latex]V_{us} = \frac{(0.87 \cdot 415 \cdot 157.08 \cdot 500)}{100} = \frac{(28302150)}{100} = 283021.5\ \text{N}[/latex] Convert to kN: [latex]V_{us} = \frac{283021.5}{1000} = \boxed{283.0\ \text{kN}}[/latex]

questions.question: The bank of a canal has the profile shown in the figure. The material is a homogeneous clay with a bulk unit weight of [latex]20\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex], undrained cohesion of [latex]30\ \text{kPa}[/latex] and it is fully saturated ([latex]\phi_u = 0[/latex]). For the trial slip circle shown, the area ABCDEA is [latex]150\ \text{m}^2[/latex] and the centroid is at P. A tension crack (DE) of [latex]2.5\ \text{m}[/latex] deep was also observed. Assume unit weight of water is [latex]9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex] and consider 1 m run of the bank for the analysis. Considering the canal is empty and the tension crack is completely filled with water, the factor of safety against slope failure of the bank is ______ (round off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
We use the concept of moment equilibrium for the slip surface. Since [latex]\phi = 0[/latex] (undrained condition), we use the following formula for factor of safety:

[latex] FS = \frac{c \cdot L}{W \cdot \frac{h}{R} - u \cdot \frac{h_w}{R}} [/latex] Where: [latex]c = 30\ \text{kPa}[/latex] (undrained cohesion) [latex]A = 150\ \text{m}^2[/latex] (area of slip mass) [latex]\gamma = 20\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex] (bulk unit weight of clay) [latex]W = \gamma \cdot A = 20 \cdot 150 = 3000\ \text{kN}[/latex] [latex]u = \gamma_w = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3[/latex] [latex]R = 14\ \text{m}[/latex] (radius of slip circle) [latex]h = h_{\text{cg}} = 2.5\ \text{m}[/latex] (vertical distance of CG from center) [latex]h_w = 2.5\ \text{m}[/latex] (depth of water in tension crack) [latex]L = \text{length of arc} = \theta \cdot R[/latex] (We don't have [latex]\theta[/latex], but can use total resisting moment and driving moment instead) Resisting moment: [latex] M_R = c \cdot A \cdot R = 30 \cdot 150 \cdot R = 4500R [/latex] Driving moment (including water pressure in tension crack): Weight moment: [latex] M_W = W \cdot h = 3000 \cdot 2.5 = 7500 [/latex] Water moment in tension crack (triangular pressure distribution): [latex] p = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \gamma_w \cdot h_w^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 9.81 \cdot (2.5)^2 = 30.65 [/latex] (acting at [latex]\frac{1}{3} \cdot 2.5 = 0.833\ \text{m}[/latex] from bottom) So moment due to water: [latex] M_u = 30.65 \cdot 0.833 \approx 25.53 [/latex] Total driving moment: [latex] M_D = 7500 + 25.53 = 7525.53 [/latex] Now, factor of safety: [latex] FS = \frac{M_R}{M_D} = \frac{4500R}{7525.53} [/latex] Substitute [latex]R = 14\ \text{m}[/latex]:

[latex] FS = \frac{4500 \cdot 14}{7525.53} = \frac{63000}{7525.53} \approx \boxed{1.07} [/latex]

(We don't have [latex]\theta[/latex], but can use total resisting moment and driving moment instead)
Resisting moment:
[latex] M_R = c \cdot A \cdot R = 30 \cdot 150 \cdot R = 4500R [/latex]
Driving moment (including water pressure in tension crack):
Weight moment:
[latex] M_W = W \cdot h = 3000 \cdot 2.5 = 7500 [/latex]
Water moment in tension crack (triangular pressure distribution):
[latex] p = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \gamma_w \cdot h_w^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 9.81 \cdot (2.5)^2 = 30.65 [/latex] (acting at [latex]\frac{1}{3} \cdot 2.5 = 0.833\ \text{m}[/latex] from bottom)

questions.question: The peak of flood hydrograph due to a 3-hour duration storm in a catchment is 180 [latex] \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex]. The total rainfall depth is 6.6 cm. The peak value of the 3-hour unit hydrograph for this catchment (in [latex] \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex]) is ______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation: Step 1: Calculate effective rainfall (runoff depth): Infiltration loss = [latex] 0.2 , \text{cm/h} [/latex] for 3 hours = [latex] 0.6 , \text{cm} [/latex] Effective rainfall = [latex] 6.6 - 0.6 = 6.0 , \text{cm} [/latex] Step 2: Calculate direct runoff peak flow: Total peak discharge = [latex] 180 , \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex] Base flow = [latex] 30 , \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex] Direct runoff peak = [latex] 180 - 30 = 150 , \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex] Step 3: Compute peak of unit hydrograph: Since the rainfall depth (i.e., runoff) corresponds to 6.0 cm, then peak of 3-hour unit hydrograph = [latex] \frac{150}{6} = 25 , \text{m}^3/\text{s} [/latex] Answer: [latex] \boxed{25 , \text{m}^3/\text{s}} [/latex]

Step 1: Calculate effective rainfall (runoff depth):
Infiltration loss = [latex] 0.2 , \text{cm/h} [/latex] for 3 hours = [latex] 0.6 , \text{cm} [/latex]

The maximum value of water depth [latex] h [/latex] (in m) that the gate can hold is __________ (round off to the nearest integer). Note: Density of water = [latex] 1000 , \text{kg/m}^3 [/latex] Acceleration due to gravity = [latex] 9.81 , \text{m/s}^2 [/latex]

The analyses results of a water sample are given below. The non-carbonate hardness of the water (in mg/L) as [latex]\text{CaCO}_3[/latex] is ______ (in integer). [latex]\text{Ca}^{2+} = 150\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex] [latex]\text{Mg}^{2+} = 40\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex] [latex]\text{Fe}^{2+} = 10\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex] [latex]\text{Na}^{+} = 50\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex] [latex]\text{K}^{+} = 10\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex] [latex]\text{CO}_3^{2-} = 120\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex] [latex]\text{HCO}_3^{-} = 30\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex] [latex]\text{Cl}^{-} = 50\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]; Other anions were not analysed.
questions.explanation: Step 1: Total hardness is caused by multivalent cations: [latex]\text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}, \text{Fe}^{2+}[/latex] [latex]\text{Total hardness} = 150 + 40 + 10 = 200\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex] Step 2: Alkalinity is contributed by [latex]\text{HCO}_3^{-}[/latex] only (because [latex]\text{CO}_3^{2-}[/latex] and [latex]\text{OH}^{-}[/latex] typically don't coexist with [latex]\text{HCO}_3^{-}[/latex] in natural water ? and presence of only 30 mg/L [latex]\text{HCO}_3^{-}[/latex] means only bicarbonate is considered). [latex]\text{Alkalinity} = 30\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex] Step 3: Carbonate hardness = [latex]\min(\text{Total hardness}, \text{Alkalinity})[/latex] [latex]\text{Carbonate hardness} = \min(200,\ 30) = 30\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex] Step 4: Non-carbonate hardness = [latex]\text{Total hardness} - \text{Carbonate hardness}[/latex] [latex]\text{Non-carbonate hardness} = 200 - 30 = \boxed{170\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3}[/latex] However, if we consider the total alkalinity as [latex]\text{CO}_3^{2-} + \text{HCO}_3^{-} = 120 + 30 = 150[/latex], then: [latex]\text{Alkalinity} = 150\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex] [latex]\text{Carbonate hardness} = \min(200,\ 150) = 150[/latex] [latex]\text{Non-carbonate hardness} = 200 - 150 = \boxed{50\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Step 1: Total hardness is caused by multivalent cations: [latex]\text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}, \text{Fe}^{2+}[/latex]
[latex]\text{Total hardness} = 150 + 40 + 10 = 200\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
Step 2: Alkalinity is contributed by [latex]\text{HCO}_3^{-}[/latex] only (because [latex]\text{CO}_3^{2-}[/latex] and [latex]\text{OH}^{-}[/latex] typically don't coexist with [latex]\text{HCO}_3^{-}[/latex] in natural water ? and presence of only 30 mg/L [latex]\text{HCO}_3^{-}[/latex] means only bicarbonate is considered).
[latex]\text{Alkalinity} = 30\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
Step 3: Carbonate hardness = [latex]\min(\text{Total hardness}, \text{Alkalinity})[/latex]
[latex]\text{Carbonate hardness} = \min(200,\ 30) = 30\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
Step 4: Non-carbonate hardness = [latex]\text{Total hardness} - \text{Carbonate hardness}[/latex]
[latex]\text{Non-carbonate hardness} = 200 - 30 = \boxed{170\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3}[/latex]
However, if we consider the total alkalinity as [latex]\text{CO}_3^{2-} + \text{HCO}_3^{-} = 120 + 30 = 150[/latex], then:
[latex]\text{Alkalinity} = 150\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3[/latex]
[latex]\text{Carbonate hardness} = \min(200,\ 150) = 150[/latex]
[latex]\text{Non-carbonate hardness} = 200 - 150 = \boxed{50\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3}[/latex]

questions.question:
A community generates 1 million litres/day (MLD) of wastewater. This wastewater is treated using an activated sludge process (ASP). The working volume of the aeration tank of the ASP is [latex]250\ \text{m}^3[/latex], and the biomass concentration in the tank is [latex]3000\ \text{mg/L}[/latex].
Analysis results showed that a biomass concentration of [latex]10\ \text{mg/L}[/latex] is present in the treated effluent from the secondary sedimentation tank of the ASP.
Sludge wastage from the system is at a rate of [latex]5000\ \text{L/day}[/latex] with a biomass concentration of [latex]10000\ \text{mg/L}[/latex].
The system is in steady-state condition. The biological sludge residence time (BSRT) of the system (in days) is ______ (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: BSRT (also called Solids Retention Time, SRT) is given by: [latex]\text{BSRT} = \frac{\text{Mass of biomass in aeration tank}}{\text{Mass of biomass leaving the system per day}}[/latex] Step 1: Biomass in aeration tank Volume = [latex]250\ \text{m}^3 = 250 \times 1000 = 250000\ \text{L}[/latex] Biomass concentration = [latex]3000\ \text{mg/L}[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \text{Mass} = 250000 \times 3000 = 750 \times 10^6\ \text{mg} = 750\ \text{kg}[/latex] Step 2: Biomass leaving the system per day Treated effluent flow = [latex]1\ \text{MLD} = 10^6\ \text{L/day}[/latex], biomass = [latex]10\ \text{mg/L}[/latex] [latex]10 \times 10^6 = 10^7\ \text{mg/day} = 10\ \text{kg/day}[/latex] Sludge wastage = [latex]5000\ \text{L/day}[/latex], biomass = [latex]10000\ \text{mg/L}[/latex] [latex]5000 \times 10000 = 5 \times 10^7\ \text{mg/day} = 50\ \text{kg/day}[/latex] Total biomass leaving per day = [latex]10 + 50 = 60\ \text{kg/day}[/latex] Step 3: BSRT calculation [latex]\text{BSRT} = \frac{750}{60} = \boxed{12.5\ \text{days}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
BSRT (also called Solids Retention Time, SRT) is given by:
[latex]\text{BSRT} = \frac{\text{Mass of biomass in aeration tank}}{\text{Mass of biomass leaving the system per day}}[/latex]

Step 1: Biomass in aeration tank
Volume = [latex]250\ \text{m}^3 = 250 \times 1000 = 250000\ \text{L}[/latex]
Biomass concentration = [latex]3000\ \text{mg/L}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \text{Mass} = 250000 \times 3000 = 750 \times 10^6\ \text{mg} = 750\ \text{kg}[/latex]

Step 2: Biomass leaving the system per day
Treated effluent flow = [latex]1\ \text{MLD} = 10^6\ \text{L/day}[/latex], biomass = [latex]10\ \text{mg/L}[/latex]
[latex]10 \times 10^6 = 10^7\ \text{mg/day} = 10\ \text{kg/day}[/latex]
Sludge wastage = [latex]5000\ \text{L/day}[/latex], biomass = [latex]10000\ \text{mg/L}[/latex]
[latex]5000 \times 10000 = 5 \times 10^7\ \text{mg/day} = 50\ \text{kg/day}[/latex]
Total biomass leaving per day = [latex]10 + 50 = 60\ \text{kg/day}[/latex]

Step 3: BSRT calculation
[latex]\text{BSRT} = \frac{750}{60} = \boxed{12.5\ \text{days}}[/latex]

questions.question: A settling chamber is used for the removal of discrete particulate matter from air with the following conditions: Horizontal velocity of air = [latex]0.2\ \text{m/s}[/latex] Temperature of air stream = [latex]77^\circ\text{C}[/latex] Specific gravity of particle to be removed = [latex]2.65[/latex] Chamber length = [latex]12\ \text{m}[/latex] Chamber height = [latex]2\ \text{m}[/latex] Viscosity of air at [latex]77^\circ\text{C} = 2.1 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{kg/m?s}[/latex] Acceleration due to gravity, [latex]g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2[/latex] Density of air at [latex]77^\circ\text{C} = 1.0\ \text{kg/m}^3[/latex] Assume the density of water as [latex]1000\ \text{kg/m}^3[/latex] and that laminar condition exists in the chamber. The minimum size of particle that will be removed with 100% efficiency in the settling chamber (in [latex]\mu m[/latex]) is ______ (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
To find the minimum size of the particle removed with 100% efficiency, we equate the settling velocity of the particle to the vertical distance the particle must settle during the residence time in the chamber.

Residence time in the chamber is: [latex] t = \frac{\text{length of chamber}}{\text{horizontal velocity}} = \frac{12}{0.2} = 60\ \text{seconds} [/latex] So, for 100% removal, the particle must fall the height of the chamber in 60 seconds: [latex] v_s = \frac{\text{height}}{t} = \frac{2}{60} = 0.0333\ \text{m/s} [/latex] Using Stokes' Law (valid under laminar conditions): [latex] v_s = \frac{g d^2 (\rho_p - \rho_f)}{18 \mu} [/latex] Where:
[latex] d = \text{diameter of particle (in m)} [/latex] [latex] \rho_p = \text{density of particle} = 2.65 \times 1000 = 2650\ \text{kg/m}^3 [/latex] [latex] \rho_f = \text{density of air} = 1.0\ \text{kg/m}^3 [/latex] [latex] \mu = \text{viscosity of air} = 2.1 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{kg/m?s} [/latex] Now solve for [latex] d [/latex]: [latex] 0.0333 = \frac{9.81 \cdot d^2 (2650 - 1)}{18 \cdot 2.1 \times 10^{-5}} [/latex] [latex] 0.0333 = \frac{9.81 \cdot d^2 \cdot 2649}{3.78 \times 10^{-4}} [/latex] [latex] d^2 = \frac{0.0333 \cdot 3.78 \times 10^{-4}}{9.81 \cdot 2649} [/latex] [latex] d^2 \approx \frac{1.25874 \times 10^{-5}}{25983.69} \approx 4.843 \times 10^{-10} [/latex] [latex] d \approx \sqrt{4.843 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m} [/latex] Convert to micrometers: [latex] d = 2.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^6 = 22.0\ \mu m [/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
To find the minimum size of the particle removed with 100% efficiency, we equate the settling velocity of the particle to the vertical distance the particle must settle during the residence time in the chamber. Residence time in the chamber is:
[latex] t = \frac{\text{length of chamber}}{\text{horizontal velocity}} = \frac{12}{0.2} = 60\ \text{seconds} [/latex]
So, for 100% removal, the particle must fall the height of the chamber in 60 seconds:
[latex] v_s = \frac{\text{height}}{t} = \frac{2}{60} = 0.0333\ \text{m/s} [/latex]
Using Stokes' Law (valid under laminar conditions):
[latex] v_s = \frac{g d^2 (\rho_p - \rho_f)}{18 \mu} [/latex]
Where: [latex] d = \text{diameter of particle (in m)} [/latex]
[latex] \rho_p = \text{density of particle} = 2.65 \times 1000 = 2650\ \text{kg/m}^3 [/latex]
[latex] \rho_f = \text{density of air} = 1.0\ \text{kg/m}^3 [/latex]
[latex] \mu = \text{viscosity of air} = 2.1 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{kg/m?s} [/latex]
Now solve for [latex] d [/latex]:
[latex] 0.0333 = \frac{9.81 \cdot d^2 (2650 - 1)}{18 \cdot 2.1 \times 10^{-5}} [/latex]
[latex] 0.0333 = \frac{9.81 \cdot d^2 \cdot 2649}{3.78 \times 10^{-4}} [/latex]
[latex] d^2 = \frac{0.0333 \cdot 3.78 \times 10^{-4}}{9.81 \cdot 2649} [/latex]
[latex] d^2 \approx \frac{1.25874 \times 10^{-5}}{25983.69} \approx 4.843 \times 10^{-10} [/latex]
[latex] d \approx \sqrt{4.843 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m} [/latex]
Convert to micrometers:
[latex] d = 2.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^6 = 22.0\ \mu m [/latex]

questions.question:
On a two-lane highway, a horizontal curve of radius [latex]300\ \text{m}[/latex] is provided.
The design speed is [latex]80\ \text{km/h}[/latex]. If the longest wheelbase of the vehicle expected on this highway is [latex]7\ \text{m}[/latex], then the extra widening required (in m) is ______ (round off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: As per IRC, extra widening on a horizontal curve is given by the formula: [latex]W_e = W_m + W_{ph}[/latex] Where: [latex]W_m = \text{mechanical widening} = \frac{n l^2}{2R}[/latex] [latex]W_{ph} = \text{psychological widening} = \frac{v}{9.5 \sqrt{R}}[/latex] Given: [latex]n = 2,\ l = 7\ \text{m},\ R = 300\ \text{m},\ v = 80\ \text{km/h}[/latex] Step 1: Mechanical Widening [latex]W_m = \frac{2 \times 7^2}{2 \times 300} = \frac{98}{600} = 0.1633\ \text{m}[/latex] Step 2: Psychological Widening [latex]\sqrt{R} = \sqrt{300} \approx 17.32[/latex] [latex]W_{ph} = \frac{80}{9.5 \times 17.32} = \frac{80}{164.54} \approx 0.4863\ \text{m}[/latex] Step 3: Total Extra Widening [latex]W_e = 0.1633 + 0.4863 = \boxed{0.65\ \text{m}}[/latex]
questions.topic: Geometric Design of Highway and Planning
questions.explanation_html:
As per IRC, extra widening on a horizontal curve is given by the formula:
[latex]W_e = W_m + W_{ph}[/latex]
Where:
[latex]W_m = \text{mechanical widening} = \frac{n l^2}{2R}[/latex]
[latex]W_{ph} = \text{psychological widening} = \frac{v}{9.5 \sqrt{R}}[/latex]

Given:
[latex]n = 2,\ l = 7\ \text{m},\ R = 300\ \text{m},\ v = 80\ \text{km/h}[/latex]

Step 1: Mechanical Widening
[latex]W_m = \frac{2 \times 7^2}{2 \times 300} = \frac{98}{600} = 0.1633\ \text{m}[/latex]

Step 2: Psychological Widening
[latex]\sqrt{R} = \sqrt{300} \approx 17.32[/latex]
[latex]W_{ph} = \frac{80}{9.5 \times 17.32} = \frac{80}{164.54} \approx 0.4863\ \text{m}[/latex]

Step 3: Total Extra Widening
[latex]W_e = 0.1633 + 0.4863 = \boxed{0.65\ \text{m}}[/latex]

questions.question: If the Fore Bearing of the lines [latex]AB[/latex] and [latex]BC[/latex] are [latex]60^\circ[/latex] and [latex]122^\circ[/latex], respectively, then the interior angle [latex]\angle ABC[/latex] (in degrees) is ______ (round off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation: To find the interior angle [latex]\angle ABC[/latex], we use the difference between: The Back Bearing of line [latex]AB[/latex], and The Fore Bearing of line [latex]BC[/latex] Step 1: Calculate Back Bearing of AB [latex] \text{FB of } AB = 60^\circ [/latex] [latex] \text{BB of } AB = 60^\circ + 180^\circ = 240^\circ [/latex] Step 2: Given Fore Bearing of BC [latex] \text{FB of } BC = 122^\circ [/latex] Step 3: Interior Angle at Point B [latex] \angle ABC = BB_{AB} - FB_{BC} = 240^\circ - 122^\circ = \boxed{118^\circ} [/latex]

questions.question: Even though I had planned to go skiing with my friends, I had to __________ at the last moment because of an injury. Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
